This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars.In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand.

Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Trump has fired his cyber director after a wave of tech outagesPentagon official Kirsten Davies will replace Sean Cairncross. (NBC News)+ The outages disrupted flights, banks and security systems. (Reuters $)+ They’ve fuelled fears of a wider collapse. (WP $)+ AI agents are expected to drive even more outages. (Politico)+ We need to monitor AI agents in real time. (MIT Technology Review)

2 The US approved sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to ChinaMany went to firms the Pentagon links to China’s military. (CNBC)+ California is investigating Nvidia’s links to China. (Politico).+ New US export rules are set to hinder Chinese AI. (WSJ $)+ Nvidia is eyeing Arm chief Rene Haas as its next CEO. (FT $)

3 The US Senate has passed a bill to fast-track energy projectsIt would cut red tape but weaken environmental protections. (Axios)+ The bill could advance Trump’s fossil-fuel agenda. (New Yorker $)+ But it could also unlock more clean energy. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Taiwan says China is using Threads to sway next week’s electionsIt has flagged nearly 2,700 suspected accounts to Meta. (Reuters $)+ Taiwan’s “silicon shield” is weakening. (MIT Technology Review)

5 Google’s AI push is hurting its search ad businessAdvertisers are shifting spending as AI answers displace ads. (NYT $)+ The agentic web is here. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Apple is building its own AI agentIt would browse the web, work across apps and write code. (Verge)+ Apple’s longtime iPhone camera chief has retired. (Bloomberg $)

7 UN climate talks are set to call for carbon removal technologiesIt could reverse warming, but the systems remain unproven. (WP $)+ Is carbon removal in trouble? (MIT Technology Review)

8 Global cooling needs have overtaken heating for the first timeHigher temperatures are driving a surge in air conditioning. (Bloomberg $)

9 GTA 6 has become the biggest entertainment launch everFirst-day sales were estimated at a record $2.3 billion. (BBC)

10 Physicists sent a message through a wall using gravity and an old liftUnlike radio signals, gravitational fields can’t be blocked by walls. (Gizmodo)

—Dingsheng Li, an environmental health professor and Anthropic investor, tells The New Yorker why he's buying into a company whose technology threatens to make human workers obsolete.

A couple of weeks ago, at a $50 million arena built in a casino parking lot in Las Vegas, I witnessed a libertarian thought experiment come to life. The inaugural Enhanced Games were the first sporting competition where participants were encouraged to take performance-enhancing drugs.

For the event’s supporters, the Enhanced Games offered a glimpse of a future where medical advances push the human race to new heights—and they never have to get old. As I watched the games unfold, two questions bounced around my head: Were they right? And what does that mean for the rest of us?

Read the full story to understand the answers.
